questions.q:
But-2-yne and hydrogen (one mole each) are separately treated with (i) Pd/C and (ii) Na/liq. NH3 to give the products X and Y respectively.
Identify the incorrect statements.
A. X and Y are stereoisomers.
B. Dipole moment of X is zero.
C. Boiling point of X is higher than Y.
D. X and Y react with O3/Zn + H2O to give different products.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explain: Here the question wants the INCORRECT statements, so read carefully. Partial hydrogenation of but-2-yne over Pd/C gives cis-but-2-ene (X) by syn addition, and Na/liq. NH3 gives trans-but-2-ene (Y) by anti addition. So X and Y are cis-trans (geometrical) isomers, which are stereoisomers, and A is correct. The cis isomer has its two C-CH3 bond dipoles on the same side, so it has a net dipole moment and B (X has zero dipole) is incorrect. The polar cis isomer has stronger dipole-dipole attraction and a higher boiling point, so C is correct. Ozonolysis of either isomer gives the same product, 2 CH3CHO, so D is incorrect. Incorrect: B and D.

questions.q: Identify (P): the vicinal dibromide shown is treated with (i) Zn, heat and then (ii) HBr to give (P), the major product.
questions.explain: Zn with heat removes two vicinal Br atoms and makes a C=C, giving a cyclopentene. One carbon of that C=C sits next to the ring carbon carrying CH3, and the other next to the ring carbon carrying the ethyl group. HBr adds H+ to one alkene carbon and gives a secondary carbocation. A 1,2-hydride shift from the neighbouring ring carbon that bears CH3 moves the charge onto it, giving a tertiary carbocation. Tertiary is more stable than secondary, so this shift happens. Br- then attacks that carbon. The major product has Br and CH3 on the same ring carbon: a tertiary bromide, with the ethyl group left on the ring. That is option D. The trap options A, B and C keep Br on a secondary carbon.

questions.q: Consider the following reaction: the dibromoalkane shown (a four-carbon chain with both Br atoms on the same carbon) + 2 NaNH2 gives X. Then X with (i) NaNH2 and (ii) isopropyl bromide gives Y. The product Y formed is:
questions.explain: Two equivalents of NaNH2 remove 2 HBr from the dibromide (double dehydrohalogenation) and give a four-carbon alkyne, X. The next NaNH2 pulls off the acidic H of a terminal alkyne to make the acetylide ion, so X must be but-1-yne, CH3CH2-C≡CH. The acetylide then attacks isopropyl bromide by SN2 and joins the isopropyl group to the triple-bond carbon. The product is CH3CH2-C≡C-CH(CH3)2. Numbering from the isopropyl end gives the methyl on C2 and the triple bond at C3, so Y is 2-methylhex-3-yne. The 2-yne options are traps: they would need the triple bond at the wrong spot. 'Isopropylbut-1-yne' is not a valid IUPAC name.

questions.q:
The incorrect statements regarding geometrical isomerism are:
A. Propene shows geometrical isomerism.
B. Trans isomer has identical atoms/groups on the opposite sides of the double bond.
C. Cis-but-2-ene has higher dipole moment than trans-but-2-ene.
D. 2-Methylbut-2-ene shows two geometrical isomers.
E. Trans-isomer has lower melting point than cis isomer.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explain: The question asks for the INCORRECT statements, so test each one. Geometrical isomerism needs two different groups on each carbon of the C=C. A (propene): the CH2 end has two H, so there is no isomerism. A is incorrect. B is the definition of the trans isomer, so it is correct. C: cis-but-2-ene has a net dipole moment and trans cancels to about zero, so C is correct. D (2-methylbut-2-ene): one carbon carries two CH3 groups, so there is no geometrical isomerism at all. D is incorrect. E: trans isomers pack better in the crystal and usually have the higher melting point, so E is incorrect. Incorrect statements: A, D and E.

questions.q: The reactions which cannot be applied to prepare an alkene by elimination, are:
questions.explain: The question asks which reactions CANNOT give an alkene by elimination, so check each one. A: a secondary bromide with a strong base (NaOEt) gives E2 elimination to 1-methylcyclohexene, so A works. B: 2-bromobutane with aqueous KOH mostly gives substitution (butan-2-ol), because elimination needs alcoholic KOH. B cannot. C: tert-butyl bromide with NaOMe gives isobutene by E2, as a tertiary halide with a strong base always eliminates. C works. D: phenol with Na2Cr2O7/H2SO4 is an oxidation (it gives benzoquinone), not an elimination. D cannot. E: a tertiary alcohol over Cu at 573 K dehydrates to isobutene. E works. So only B and D cannot. Correct: B & D only.

questions.q: The incorrect statement regarding the geometrical isomers of 2-butene is:
options: cis-2-butene and trans-2-butene are not interconvertible at room temperature.
cis-2-butene has less dipole moment than trans-2-butene.
trans-2-butene is more stable than cis-2-butene.
questions.explain: You need the false statement, so test each one. The two 2-butenes differ only in how the groups sit around the C=C, so they are stereoisomers (geometrical isomers). The C=C double bond cannot rotate at room temperature, so they do not interconvert, and the first statement is true. In the trans isomer the two CH3 groups are on opposite sides, so there is less steric crowding and it is more stable than cis. That statement is true. Dipole moment is where the trap is. In cis, the two C-CH3 bond dipoles add up, so cis has a net dipole moment. In trans they cancel almost completely, so the dipole moment is about zero. So cis has MORE dipole moment than trans, and the statement that cis has less is the incorrect one.

questions.q: The least acidic compound, among the following, is:
questions.explain: Compare how easily each compound gives up its acidic H, since the weaker the acid, the harder that is. The sulfonic acid (benzenesulfonic acid) is the strongest here, a very strong acid because its conjugate base is stabilised by three S=O/O- resonance forms. The carboxylic acid (butanoic acid) is next, with pKa about 4.8 and a resonance-stabilised carboxylate. 3-Ethoxyphenol is a phenol, with pKa about 10. The only acidic H in ethyl propiolate is the terminal alkyne C-H (EtO2C-C≡C-H). Its pKa is about 25 even with the ester pulling electrons, so it is by far the weakest acid. It is not a carboxylic acid despite having an ester. Least acidic: ethyl propiolate, option A.

questions.q: The ascending acidity order of the following H atoms (circled in the structures) is:
questions.explain: Acidity of a C-H bond depends on the s-character of the carbon, because an sp carbon holds the lone pair of its conjugate base closer to the nucleus. The H in A is on an sp carbon (a terminal alkyne), which is the most acidic. The H in B is on an sp2 carbon (vinylic), which is less acidic. In C and D the H is on an sp3 carbon (alkanes), which are the least acidic. Between the two alkanes, the conjugate base of the tertiary (C) carbanion is destabilised by three electron-donating CH3 groups, while the primary one (D) is destabilised less. So C is less acidic than D. Ascending order: C < D < B < A.

questions.q: Cyclohexene (structure shown) is _______ type of an organic compound.
questions.explain: Start with how organic compounds are classified. Acyclic means open-chain, with no ring. Cyclic compounds have a ring. Within cyclic, aromatic compounds are benzene-like, with a ring that has delocalised pi electrons (4n+2 rule). Alicyclic compounds are rings that behave like aliphatic compounds. Cyclohexene has a six-membered ring, so it is not acyclic. It has only one C=C, and the other four ring carbons are sp3, so the ring is not conjugated around its whole circle, and it is not aromatic. So it is an alicyclic compound. 'Benzenoid' also means a benzene ring is present, which cyclohexene does not have. The trap is thinking any ring with a double bond is aromatic.
